3.2 Significant-subspace Alignment

In this section, we describe our method, Significant-subspace Alignment (SSA), to tackle the aforementioned problem of naive feature alignment. Fig. 1 shows an overview of SSA. As described in Sec. 3.1, the features of a regression model tend to be distributed in a small subspace of the feature space. Thus, we introduce subspace detection to detect a subspace that is representative and significant to the output and then perform feature alignment in the subspace. Subspace detection is similar to principal component analysis (PCA). Further, in our regression model, a feature 𝐳=gϕ​(𝐱)\mathbf{z}=g_{\phi}(\mathbf{x}) is projected onto a one-dimensional line determined by 𝐰\mathbf{w} of hψh_{\psi} in order to output a scalar value 𝐰⊤​𝐳+b\mathbf{w}^{\top}\mathbf{z}+b. Thus, a subspace basis 𝐯ds\mathbf{v}^{\text{s}}_{d} whose direction is not orthogonal to 𝐰\mathbf{w} needs precise feature alignment. We use dimension weighting to prioritize such dimensions.

Subspace detection. After the training on the source dataset 𝒮\mathcal{S}, we detect the subspace in which the source features are distributed. Instead of computing the variance of each dimension as Eqs. 1 and 2, we compute the covariance matrix:

𝚺s=1Ns​∑i=1Ns(𝐳is−𝝁s)​(𝐳is−𝝁s)⊤,\bm{\Sigma}^{\text{s}}=\frac{1}{N_{\text{s}}}\sum_{i=1}^{N_{\text{s}}}(\mathbf{z}_{i}^{\text{s}}-\bm{\mu}^{\text{s}})(\mathbf{z}_{i}^{\text{s}}-\bm{\mu}^{\text{s}})^{\top}, (5)

where the source mean vector 𝝁s\bm{\mu}^{\text{s}} is the same as Eqs. 1 and 2.

Then, we detect the source subspace. On the basis of PCA, the subspace is spanned by the eigenvectors of the covariance matrix 𝚺s\bm{\Sigma}^{\text{s}}, denoted by 𝐯ks\mathbf{v}_{k}^{\text{s}} (‖𝐯ks‖2=1\|\mathbf{v}_{k}^{\text{s}}\|_{2}=1). The corresponding eigenvalues λks\lambda_{k}^{\text{s}} represent the variance of the source features along the direction 𝐯ks\mathbf{v}_{k}^{\text{s}}. We use the top-KK largest eigenvalues λ1s,…,λKs​(λ1s>⋯>λKs)\lambda_{1}^{\text{s}},\ldots,\lambda_{K}^{\text{s}}~(\lambda_{1}^{\text{s}}>\cdots>\lambda_{K}^{\text{s}}), the corresponding source bases 𝐯1s,…,𝐯Ks\mathbf{v}_{1}^{\text{s}},\ldots,\mathbf{v}_{K}^{\text{s}}, and the source mean 𝝁s\bm{\mu}^{\text{s}} as the source statistics.

Dimension weighting. Since we assume that the output is computed with a linear regressor hψ​(𝐳)=𝐰⊤​𝐳+bh_{\psi}(\mathbf{z})=\mathbf{w}^{\top}\mathbf{z}+b, the effect of a subspace dimension 𝐯ds\mathbf{v}^{\text{s}}_{d} to the output is determined by 𝐰⊤​𝐯ds\mathbf{w}^{\top}\mathbf{v}^{\text{s}}_{d}. To prioritize the subspace dimensions that have larger effect on the output, we determine the weight of each subspace dimension as follows:

αd=1+|𝐰⊤​𝐯ds|.\alpha_{d}=1+|\mathbf{w}^{\top}\mathbf{v}^{\text{s}}_{d}|. (6)

αd\alpha_{d} assigns a larger weight when the direction along a subspace basis 𝐯ds\mathbf{v}_{d}^{\text{s}} affects the output, or keep the weight to one when not.

Feature alignment. This step is done in the target domain. Given a target mini-batch ℬ\mathcal{B} sampled from the target dataset 𝒯\mathcal{T}, we project the target features 𝐳it=gϕ​(𝐱it)\mathbf{z}_{i}^{\text{t}}=g_{\phi}(\mathbf{x}_{i}^{\text{t}}) into the source subspace and then compute the feature alignment loss. The projection of the target feature is computed as follows:

𝐳~it=𝐕s​(𝐳it−𝝁s),\tilde{\mathbf{z}}_{i}^{\text{t}}=\mathbf{V}^{\text{s}}(\mathbf{z}_{i}^{\text{t}}-\bm{\mu}^{\text{s}}), (7)

where 𝐕s=[𝐯1s,…,𝐯Ks]⊤∈ℝK×D\mathbf{V}^{\text{s}}=[\mathbf{v}_{1}^{\text{s}},\ldots,\mathbf{v}_{K}^{\text{s}}]^{\top}\in\mathbb{R}^{K\times D}. With 𝐳~it∈ℝK\tilde{\mathbf{z}}^{\text{t}}_{i}\in\mathbb{R}^{K}, we compute the projected target mean and variance over the mini-batch analogously to Eqs. 1 and 2; this is denoted by 𝝁~t{\tilde{\bm{\mu}}^{\text{t}}} and 𝝈~t 2\tilde{\bm{\sigma}}^{\text{t~2}}. On the other hand, the projected source mean and variance are 𝟎\mathbf{0} and the eigenvalues 𝝀s=[λ1s,…,λKs]\bm{\lambda}^{\text{s}}=[\lambda_{1}^{\text{s}},\ldots,\lambda_{K}^{\text{s}}] since 𝚺s​𝐯ks=λks​𝐯ks\bm{\Sigma^{\text{s}}}\mathbf{v}_{k}^{\text{s}}=\lambda^{\text{s}}_{k}\mathbf{v}_{k}^{\text{s}}. (8)

During TTA, we optimize the feature extractor gϕg_{\phi} to minimize ℒTTA\mathcal{L}_{\text{TTA}}, i.e., we seek ϕ∗=minϕ⁡ℒTTA​(ϕ)\phi^{*}=\min_{\phi}\mathcal{L}_{\text{TTA}}(\phi). We update only the affine parameters γ\gamma and β\beta of the normalization layers such as batch normalization [26] or layer normalization [2] inspired by Tent [54]. This strategy is effective not only to avoid forgetting the source knowledge but also to enable flexible adaptation [20, 5]. The procedure of SSA is listed in Algorithm 1 of the Appendix.

On the other hand, RSD [6] is originally designed for regression in UDA but did not work in the California Housing dataset because of numerical instability of SVD performed on every target feature batch. In contrast, our method is stable since it avoids degenerated dimensions during TTA. Tab. 4 shows the R2R^{2} scores on the UTKFace with image corruption. We can see that SSA had the highest R2R^{2} scores for most of the corruption types. In particular, SSA outperformed the baselines by a large margin on noise-type corruption which significantly degraded the performance of Source. Tab. 5 shows the R2R^{2} scores on Biwi Kinect with genders different from the source domains. SSA constantly had higher R2R^{2} scores than the baselines; the baselines’ scores sometimes significantly dropped or even diverged (Prototype). In summary, SSA consistently improved the scores whereas the baselines sometimes even underperformed Source. Moreover, SSA worked well not only on image data but also tabular data.
